title: A lookbook that still leads to a product
metaTitle: A lookbook that reaches a product
excerpt: A lookbook can carry a story if every scene that shows an object links to that object, with a name and a price. A film with no path is a mood, not a shop.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk. The notes are the path a lookbook scene still has to provide.
caption: A page with a note you can actually read. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does a lookbook need a buy button on every frame?
faqs.answer: It needs a path from each object in the frame to that object's product page, with the shop's name and the price. One button labeled shop the story, pointing at a whole grid, makes the person hunt for the coat they just saw. Three objects in a frame means three links.

faqs.question: Can a lookbook include a sold-out piece?
faqs.answer: Only if the caption says it is gone and the page it links to tells the truth. A beautiful frame that lands on a dead purchase button undoes the story. Swap in a color you can sell, or say the piece will not return.

faqs.question: What should the page title say?
faqs.answer: Name the collection or the season, and keep the brand, so a tab and a search result describe the page. A title that only says Journal or Stories throws away the glance. The story can stay atmospheric. The title should still say what room this is.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in Google Search

markdown:
Lookbook website design can carry a story and still be a shop. Every scene that shows an object should reach that object: a name, a price, and a way to the product page. A film with no path is a mood. People can enjoy a mood and still leave without knowing what you sell.

Start with the object the photograph actually contains. Then write the sentence that connects it to the product a person can buy, save, or ask about. If you cannot name the object, the frame does not belong in the shop.

## A scene is a path, not a poster

A lookbook earns its place when it helps someone recognize the object in use and then find it without a search. The frame, the caption, and the link are one unit. Break any of them and the page becomes a gallery that happens to share a logo with the store.

People do not give a vague page much time. Nielsen Norman Group, in Jakob Nielsen’s 2011 piece on [how long users stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), reports that users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that you need a clear value proposition inside the first 10 seconds to earn longer attention. A lookbook’s value proposition is specific. This is the collection, these are the pieces, here is how to look closer. An opening frame with no words spends that window on atmosphere alone.

Put the collection name and one plain sentence above the first image. “Autumn delivery. Outerwear, knits, and the bag we cut in the same cloth.” Then the images. The sentence is not a manifesto. It is how a stranger knows they are in a shop and not in a mood film that forgot its door.

Google’s guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that describe the page clearly. A lookbook title that is only “Journal” or “Stories” throws away the query and the glance in a tab. Name the season or the collection, and keep the brand, so the result and the tab tell the truth about where the link goes.

## What every frame owes the reader

For each scene, write a caption a person can act on.

- The product name, as it appears in the shop
- The price, or “sold as a set” if that is the truth
- One detail the photo cannot carry: cloth, fit, or what the object is for
- A link on the name, or a clear control, to the product page

If the frame contains three objects, it contains three links, or it is the wrong frame for a shop. A single “shop the story” button that dumps someone on a category grid forces them to hunt for the coat they just saw. Shop the scene means a list of the objects in the scene.

Crop is part of the path. If the object is unrecognizable, the link feels like a bait. Show enough of the thing that the product photograph on the next page is obviously the same thing. Color and scale are the usual breaks. A lookbook crop that reads black, linking to a product photo that is navy, will feel like a mistake even when both are honest.

Out-of-stock objects can appear only with the status in the caption. A dreamy frame of a sold-out piece, linked to a dead button, undoes the care you spent on the story. Say it is gone, and link anyway if the page explains the return, or swap in the color you can sell.

## Story is welcome when it stays attached

A paragraph about the shoot, the place, or the reason the collection exists can sit between scenes. Keep it short enough that the objects still arrive before a restless reader leaves. The story should name the objects it depends on. “The coat on the ferry” only works if the coat is identified and linked where that sentence appears.

Video can do the same job if the type and the link survive it. A full-bleed film with no captions is a dead end on a phone, where the controls are easy to miss. Offer a still path beside the film: the same objects, listed, for the person who will not wait for the frame they wanted. Sound should be off until they ask for it. A lookbook that shouts on load will be closed before the first product appears.

Do not invent a narrative the product cannot keep. If the copy says the bag is waxed canvas and the product page says nylon, the story has become a defect. The lookbook and the product page share one set of facts. The lookbook is allowed to be more atmospheric. It is not allowed to be more fictional.

Editorial brands already know this discipline. Thomas Bewick’s public site is an editorial heritage project, where the reading and the object have to belong together. The same standard helps a younger shop. If a sentence does not point at something you sell or something you believe that the product page repeats, cut the sentence.

## The grid under the story

After the scenes, or beside them on a wide screen, give a plain list of everything the lookbook featured. Name, price, availability, link. This is the page for the person who scrolled for a feeling and is now ready to choose. It is also the page your team can check against the shop. If a product is in the film and missing from the list, the film is unfinished.

Order the list the way you want the collection remembered, not the way the camera happened to pan. Lead with the object you cut the story around. Group by category only if the lookbook is long enough to need it. A list of eight does not need a filter.

Each row should use the shop’s product name, not the stylist’s nickname. Nicknames can live in the caption as flavor. The link text should be the name a person can find again in search and in the receipt. Consistency here is what makes the lookbook part of the store instead of a side project the store does not recognize.

When a product leaves the collection, take it out of the list and decide what the scene should do. Leaving a link to a discontinued page with no status is how old campaigns keep spending trust. Update the scene or retire the page. A dated lookbook that is honest about being past is fine. A dated lookbook that still says “buy” is not.

## Photography, credit, and the file you keep

Direct the photographs for recognition first and mood second. Full looks are useful when each piece is called out. Detail crops are useful when the detail is the reason to buy, and the product is already named. A crop of a texture with no product name is a screensaver.

Keep the set in one place your team can find after the launch week. The client portal, when a Hanabi project uses one, is where brand files and updates live after delivery. A lookbook that depends on a folder in someone’s downloads will lose the frame you need when a product returns. Name files with the product, not with the camera’s number.

Alt text should describe the picture: who or what is in the frame, and which garment or object is visible. Do not stuff the caption with slogans. The caption carries the shop link. The alt text carries the scene. They are different sentences for different readers, including someone who does not see the image.

Credit the photographer in the colophon of the lookbook if that was the agreement. A credit line does not replace the product link. It sits at the end, quiet, after the shop has done its job.

## A lookbook that knows it is not the homepage

The homepage can point at the current lookbook. The lookbook should not be forced to do the homepage’s whole job: every category, every policy, every announcement. One story, one collection, a way into the products, and a way back to the shop. If you have three stories, you have three pages, each with its own list.

Measure the page by the path, not by how long someone stared. A useful check is whether a person who saw a specific object can reach its product page in one tap from the scene, and whether that product page shows the same name and a price. If the answer is no, the lookbook is still a film.

Seasonal pages should be linked from the current season and left alone once they are archived, with a line at the top if the products have changed. Do not delete URLs that campaigns still use. Correct them. A corrected archive that says the collection has moved, and links to what you can buy now, keeps the old story without pretending it is the shop today.

Gift cards and other simple extras often get forgotten at the edge of a beautiful story page, then surface as a broken footer link. [Gift cards and the simple version](/blog/gift-cards-and-the-simple-version) is the next piece if your lookbook is in good shape and the small utilities around the shop are not.
